questions.question: What is the frequency counting pattern and when do you apply it?
questions.title: Frequency Counting Pattern Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Frequency counting** uses a HashMap or array to count occurrences of elements in O(n) time. Apply it when a problem asks about duplicates, most-common elements, or character frequencies — it avoids the O(n²) of nested comparison loops.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you recognize counting-based problems and reach for the right data structure immediately
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing a nested loop for frequency problems when a single HashMap pass solves it in O(n)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name 4+ problems that use this pattern and show the template code structure

sections.title: Count Once, Query Fast
sections.content: **Template**: iterate input once, building `Map<Element, Integer> freq`. Each element: `freq.merge(e, 1, Integer::sum)`. Then query the map in O(1) per lookup. Problems that use this: anagram check (compare two freq maps), first non-repeating character (first char with count 1), majority element (count > n/2), top-k frequent elements (sort entries by value), group anagrams (sort chars as map key).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Build: O(n) single pass with getOrDefault or merge
- Query: O(1) per lookup
- int[26]: faster for lowercase letter problems
- HashMap: general purpose for any element type
- Anagram: two frequency maps must be equal
- First unique: iterate string again, find first with count 1
- Majority element: count > n/2 (or use Boyer-Moore for O(1) space)
- Top-k: use PriorityQueue on Map.Entry sorted by value

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The frequency counting pattern is my first thought when I see a problem involving duplicates, counts, or character occurrences. I do one pass through the input to build a frequency map, then query it as needed. The build is O(n) and queries are O(1). For character problems I'll use an int array of size 26 for speed; for general elements I use a HashMap. It underlies anagram detection, finding the first non-repeating character, majority element, and top-k frequency problems. Once you recognize the pattern it simplifies many problems that look complex.

questions.question: How do you find the top K most frequent elements in an array?
questions.title: Top K Frequent Elements Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Build a frequency map, then use a min-heap of size k.** Iterate map entries — if heap size < k, add; if the current frequency > heap top's frequency, replace the top. Final heap contains the k most frequent elements. O(n log k) time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Combining frequency map with a heap — a very common interview combination
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sorting all elements by frequency (O(n log n)) when the problem only asks for top k — a heap gives O(n log k) which is better
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why a min-heap of size k is more efficient than a max-heap or full sort

sections.title: Frequency Map + Min-Heap of Size K
sections.content: Step 1: build `Map<Integer,Integer> freq` in O(n). Step 2: create `PriorityQueue<Map.Entry>` ordered by value (frequency) ascending — min-heap. Iterate map entries: offer entry to heap; if heap size > k, poll (removes the entry with smallest frequency). After processing all entries, heap contains exactly k most frequent elements. **Why min-heap**: we want to efficiently discard the least frequent element when we exceed k.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Step 1: frequency map — O(n)
- Step 2: min-heap of size k — O(n log k)
- Total: O(n log k) — better than O(n log n) sort when k << n
- PriorityQueue comparator: Comparator.comparingInt(Map.Entry::getValue)
- Alternative: bucket sort — O(n) using index as frequency
- Bucket sort: create List[] of size n+1, put elements at their frequency index
- Extract top k from highest non-empty buckets

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I use two steps. First, build a frequency map in O(n). Second, use a min-heap of size k over the map entries. For each entry, I add it to the heap. If the heap size exceeds k, I poll the minimum frequency entry out. This keeps only the k highest frequencies in the heap. The total complexity is O(n log k) which is better than sorting all n entries in O(n log n), especially when k is much smaller than n. I'd also mention the bucket sort alternative which achieves O(n) by using frequency as the array index.

questions.question: How do you group strings that are anagrams together?
questions.title: Group Anagrams Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Sort each string's characters as a key, grouping strings with the same sorted key.** Use `HashMap<String, List<String>>`. Sorting 'eat' → 'aet', 'tea' → 'aet', 'ate' → 'aet' — they all map to the same key. O(n * k log k) where k = max string length.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can design an appropriate canonical key for grouping — the 'sorted string' insight
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Checking all pairs with isAnagram() — O(n² * k) instead of the O(n * k log k) grouping approach
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the alternative key using character frequency array converted to string (e.g., '1a2b' format) — avoids sorting, O(n*k)

sections.title: Canonical Form as HashMap Key
sections.content: Two strings are anagrams iff they have the same character multiset. **Key insight**: define a canonical form that all anagrams share. **Approach 1**: sort each string's characters — 'eat', 'tea', 'ate' all become 'aet'. **Approach 2**: build a char frequency array, convert to a string key — avoids sorting. `Map<String, List<String>> map`; for each string compute its canonical key and `map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(s)`. Return `new ArrayList<>(map.values())`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Sort approach: key = sorted char array as String — O(k log k) per string
- Frequency approach: key = int[26] as String — O(k) per string, no sort
- computeIfAbsent: clean idiom for list-valued maps
- Total sort approach: O(n * k log k)
- Total frequency approach: O(n * k)
- Return map.values() as the list of groups
- Empty string edge case: sorts to empty string, valid group

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The key insight is that all anagrams of each other share the same canonical form. I sort each string's characters to get that canonical form — 'eat', 'tea', and 'ate' all become 'aet'. I use this as a HashMap key mapping to a list of original strings. For each input string I compute its sorted key and add it to the corresponding list using computeIfAbsent. At the end I return the map's values. This is O(n times k log k). I'd also mention a slightly faster approach using a character frequency array as the key, which avoids sorting and makes it O(n times k).

questions.question: How do you find the first non-repeating character in a string?
questions.title: First Non-Repeating Character Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Two passes: first build a frequency map, then scan the string to find the first character with count 1.** Using LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order but a simple int[26] with a second scan is more common. O(n) time, O(1) space for alphabet input.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic frequency map application — straightforward but tests clean two-pass thinking
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using nested loops — O(n²) — instead of the two-pass O(n) approach
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Queue-based approach for streaming input where you can't do two passes

sections.title: Two-Pass: Count Then Scan
sections.content: **Pass 1**: build frequency count — `int[26] count`; for each char: `count[c - 'a']++`. **Pass 2**: iterate the original string in order; return the first character where `count[c - 'a'] == 1`. Return '#' or -1 if none found. **Why second pass on string and not map**: maps don't preserve input order (HashMap); we need to find the first occurrence in the original order, so we scan the string again.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Pass 1: build frequency — O(n)
- Pass 2: find first with count 1 — O(n)
- Total: O(n) time, O(1) space (fixed 26-char array)
- Second pass must be on string, not map (preserve order)
- LinkedHashMap alternative: one pass + iterate entries in insertion order
- Index approach: store first occurrence index in map, find min index with count 1
- Streaming: use a queue of unique characters, update front on new duplicates

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I use two passes. First pass: count the frequency of each character using an int array of size 26. Second pass: iterate the original string again and return the first character whose count in the array is exactly one. The second pass must be on the string, not the frequency map, because I need to preserve the original order. This is O(n) time and O(1) space since the array is a fixed size. A common follow-up is the streaming version where you can't see the whole string at once — for that I'd use a queue that tracks the current unique characters, removing from the front when they become duplicates.

questions.question: How do you use frequency counting to check if a string can be rearranged into a palindrome?
questions.title: Can a String Be Rearranged into a Palindrome? Frequency Counting Approach
questions.direct_answer: Count the frequency of each character; the string can form a palindrome only if at most one character has an odd frequency — that character would occupy the center position.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the mathematical property of palindromes and can map it to a frequency-counting check
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that strings with odd length are allowed exactly one odd-frequency character
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the int[26] array instead of a HashMap for lowercase letters and explain why it is faster

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I start with the key insight: in a palindrome, every character must appear an even number of times so it can be mirrored on both sides. The only exception is the middle character of an odd-length palindrome, which can appear an odd number of times. So the rule is: a string can be rearranged into a palindrome if and only if at most one character has an odd frequency.

For the implementation I use an int array of size 26 since we are dealing with lowercase letters. I iterate through the string and increment the count at index (char - 'a') for each character. Then I count how many entries in the array are odd. If that odd count is greater than one, I return false; otherwise I return true.

Using int[26] instead of a HashMap avoids hashing overhead — lookups and updates are O(1) array accesses and the space is always constant at 26 integers.

I always walk the interviewer through the two examples: 'aab' → frequencies a=2, b=1 → one odd count → can form 'aba', valid. 'abc' → a=1, b=1, c=1 → three odd counts → cannot form a palindrome.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Palindrome property: at most one character may have an odd frequency
Use int[26] for lowercase letters: freq[ch - 'a']++
Count how many array entries are odd; if > 1 → return false
O(n) time, O(1) space (26-entry array is constant)
Works for both even-length and odd-length palindromes

followup_questions: How would you handle uppercase letters or Unicode characters?

questions.question: How do you find the top K frequent elements using a HashMap and heap?
questions.title: Top K Frequent Elements Using HashMap and Min-Heap
questions.direct_answer: Build a frequency map with a HashMap, then maintain a min-heap of size K — add each entry and evict the minimum when the heap exceeds K, leaving the K most frequent elements.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to combine two data structures — HashMap for counting and PriorityQueue for selection
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a max-heap of all elements (O(n log n)) instead of a min-heap of size K (O(n log k))
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why a min-heap of size K is more efficient than sorting the entire frequency map

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The algorithm has two phases: counting and selecting.

In the counting phase, I iterate through the array and build a HashMap where the key is the element and the value is its frequency. This takes O(n) time.

In the selection phase, I use a PriorityQueue configured as a min-heap ordered by frequency. I iterate over every entry in the map. If the heap has fewer than K elements I add the entry immediately. If the heap already has K elements and the current entry's frequency is greater than the frequency at the top of the heap — the minimum — I remove the top and add the current entry. After processing all map entries, the K entries remaining in the heap are the K most frequent.

The reason I use a min-heap rather than a max-heap is efficiency. A min-heap of size K only needs O(log K) for each insertion and eviction, giving O(n log K) total. If I sorted the entire map by frequency it would be O(n log n), which is worse when K is small.

I mention that Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default, and I pass a comparator like `Comparator.comparingInt(e -> e.getValue())` to order by frequency.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Phase 1: HashMap to count frequencies — O(n)
Phase 2: min-heap (PriorityQueue) of size K, ordered by frequency
Add entry if heap.size() < K; else if freq > heap.peek().freq → poll and add
O(n log K) time — better than O(n log n) sorting when K << n
